articles.title: One env var between localhost and production: how VITE_API_URL keeps my axios client deploy-proof
articles.excerpt: I once shipped a frontend with http://localhost:8000/api hardcoded in the axios client. It worked perfectly — on my machine. The production build called localhost on every user's browser, failed silen…
articles.body: I once shipped a frontend with http://localhost:8000/api hardcoded in the axios client. It worked perfectly — on my machine. The production build called localhost on every user's browser, failed silently, and I spent an evening learning about CORS before realizing the actual bug was a string literal. The rule now: the API base URL comes from exactly one env var, with a sane fallback. Nothing else in the frontend knows the backend's address. // .env.example VITE_API_URL = http : //localhost:8000 const client = isDemoMode () ? createDemoClient () : axios . create ({ baseURL : ` ${ import . meta . env .

articles.title: PostgreSQL 19 Slips to November as AI Code Review Finds Bugs Faster Than Humans Can Fix Them
articles.excerpt: PostgreSQL 19 Slips to November as AI Code Review Finds Bugs Faster Than Humans Can Fix Them The PostgreSQL Global Development Group has delayed PostgreSQL 19, pushing general availability from the or…
articles.body: PostgreSQL 19 Slips to November as AI Code Review Finds Bugs Faster Than Humans Can Fix Them The PostgreSQL Global Development Group has delayed PostgreSQL 19, pushing general availability from the original late-September/early-October target to around November 19, 2026 — and the culprit, remarkably, is not sloppy engineering. It is the opposite: AI-assisted code review has become so effective that it is finding problems faster than the volunteer-driven project can fix them. According to a detailed account from leading PostgreSQL committer Peter Eisentraut, VP at support and consultancy firm EDB, the release team has reverted somewhere between eight and ten significant features from PostgreSQL 19, deferring them to PostgreSQL 20.
articles.author: TechPulse

articles.title: My users table reads one pagination contract: paginate(15), withQueryString, and a React pager that trusts meta
articles.excerpt: The first admin panel I built fetched all users, dumped them into state, and sliced pages client-side. It worked until a client hit 2,000 users and the list page took eleven seconds to load. Server-si…
articles.body: The first admin panel I built fetched all users, dumped them into state, and sliced pages client-side. It worked until a client hit 2,000 users and the list page took eleven seconds to load. Server-side pagination isn't hard. The hard part is agreeing on the contract between Laravel and React so neither side improvises. On the backend, the users index is four lines of intent: $users = User :: query () -> latest () -> paginate ( 15 ) -> withQueryString (); return UserResource :: collection ( $users ); paginate(15) does the heavy lifting — limit, offset, total count. withQueryString() appends the current query string to the links Laravel generates, so any future filters I add (search, role) survive a page change.

articles.title: How I built a live halftone portrait in React with just Canvas 2D
articles.excerpt: My portfolio is set like a newspaper, so my photo couldn't just be a photo. I wanted it to look like a printed halftone: a grid of dots, bigger where the picture is dark and smaller where it's light.…
articles.body: My portfolio is set like a newspaper, so my photo couldn't just be a photo. I wanted it to look like a printed halftone: a grid of dots, bigger where the picture is dark and smaller where it's light. And I wanted it to be alive, so the dots swell and get pushed away when you move the cursor over them. It turned out to be about 150 lines of React and plain Canvas 2D, with no dependencies. Here's how it works. Step 1: turn the image into a grid of samples A halftone is just a low-resolution version of the picture drawn with dots. So the first job is to shrink the image to roughly one pixel per dot and read the pixels back.

articles.title: Pushing Beats Polling Explained: Live Poll Trust Above a Handful of Viewers
articles.excerpt: Short answer: pushing beats polling above a handful of viewers because one state change should not trigger repeated reads for every screen, but treat delivery as an optimization, not as authorization.…
articles.body: Short answer: pushing beats polling above a handful of viewers because one state change should not trigger repeated reads for every screen, but treat delivery as an optimization, not as authorization. Scope every subscription token to one session, keep vote acceptance on a trusted server path, and retain a slow refresh route for recovery. Polling is operationally attractive at first because its failure mode is obvious; its repeated reads, synchronized timers, and stale windows become the wrong load shape as viewership grows. This is a capacity decision before it is a pricing decision. The cost mechanism is explained by duplicated work, not by a vendor's changing unit price.
articles.author: LiamFoster1844

articles.title: Why we stopped retrying on timeout and built reconciliation instead
articles.excerpt: Early in StareBrain’s action dispatch layer, we had a simple rule: if an action times out, retry it. It felt safe. It felt standard. It was wrong. The problem isn’t the retry. The problem is what a ti…
articles.body: Early in StareBrain’s action dispatch layer, we had a simple rule: if an action times out, retry it. It felt safe. It felt standard. It was wrong. The problem isn’t the retry. The problem is what a timeout actually tells you — which is almost nothing. What a timeout means (and doesn’t mean) When a dispatch call times out, you know one thing: you didn’t get a response in time. That’s it. You don’t know whether the action reached the provider. You don’t know whether it executed. You don’t know whether it’s sitting in a queue about to execute in the next 200ms. Retrying in that state doesn’t solve the ambiguity. It doubles it. Now you have two dispatches in flight and still no confirmed outcome for either. For a calendar booking, that means two bookings. For a payment, two charges.

articles.body: I used to think being interested in the night sky meant I had to try every meteor shower. If a calendar said "peak," I interpreted that as an instruction. I'd set an alarm, find several layers of clothing and go outside at around 2:00 a.m. when even the neighborhood cats seemed surprised to see me. Then I'd spend an increasingly resentful 45 minutes staring upward, occasionally see one meteor and wonder whether I was somehow doing it all wrong. As I've grown into stargazing, I've become much more selective. The Orionids peak next week, and normally I'd be tempted. These fast meteors come from debris from Halley's Comet , which is enough of a connection to make almost anyone want to go outside.

articles.body: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have unraveled some of the atmospheric secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot world that has the consistency of marshmallow. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , under the watchful infrared eye of the JWST , is WASP-17b, located around 1,300 light-years away. The exoplanet has a mass around 0.8 times that of Jupiter, but it is around twice as wide as the solar system's largest planet, giving it a "super-puff" consistency comparable to the Earth-based treat. WASP-17 b is so close to its parent star that it completes an orbit in under four Earth days, with this proximity also making the temperature of this " hot Jupiter " skyrocket.

articles.excerpt: The Orionids peak around Oct. 21. Here's when and where to look for the best chance of spotting meteors.
articles.body: If you love watching meteors, 2026 has given you plenty to enjoy. This summer, the annual Perseid meteor shower peaked on the day of a new moon — and a solar eclipse — so moonlight stayed out of the way. And there's more to look forward to: in December, the Geminids, the year's most prolific shower, will peak after a waxing crescent moon sets early in the evening, opening the door to excellent viewing. Right between those two headline showers, the dependable Orionids take their turn, reaching peak activity around Oct. 21-22. So, when and where can you catch the show? When and where to watch Make sure you wrap up warm for a night of Orionid hunting.

articles.title: SpaceX thrusters just made a Tesla Roadster 'fly' (and Elon Musk's car is still out there in space)
articles.excerpt: Tesla just unveiled its new Roadster with a spectacular stunt, using SpaceX thrusters to make the sleek vehicle "fly."
articles.body: Well, that was a memorable debut. Tesla unveiled its highly anticipated new Roadster last night (Oct. 16) with a spectacular stunt, using SpaceX thrusters to make the vehicle "fly." "This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car, OK?" Elon Musk , who runs both companies, said during the livestreamed reveal, which was held at SpaceX's rocket-testing facility in McGregor, Texas. "But it takes the the fun meter to 11 out of 10." Tesla's next-gen, thruster-equipped Roadster launches itself over other vehicles during an unveiling event on Oct. 15, 2026. (Image credit: Tesla) Tesla first announced the next-gen Roadster in 2017, saying at the time that it would be released in 2020 . In 2018, Musk announced that the new car would incorporate some SpaceX tech.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 16, 1975: NASA launches the 1st-ever GOES weather satellite to watch Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES weather satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES satellite! GOES-A was the first in a series of weather satellites that NASA jointly operated with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The name is short for Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite . GOES-A launched on a Delta rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida. GOES satellites all have a geostationary orbit, which means they always face the same part of Earth — in this case, the Indian Ocean. Once GOES-A became operational, it was renamed GOES-1. The GOES satellite fleet has grown over the years, and is a critical link in the chain of satellites tracking Earth's weather from space.
